subtopics.name: Effect of Ligand Exchange on Stability Constant

parts.problem_md:
Nickel(II) ions, Ni<sup>2+</sup> (aq), react with a variety of ligands to form octahedral complexes.

i) Define the term stability constant, *K*<sub>stab</sub>

[2]

Nickel(II) ions react with an excess of aqueous ammonia to form the complex ion [Ni(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>.

ii) Write an expression for the stability constant, *K*<sub>stab</sub>, for this complex.

[1]

*K*<sub>stab</sub> =
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The stability constant, *K*<sub>stab</sub>, is:
> 
> - The equilibrium constant for the formation of a complex ion (from a central metal ion and its ligands) **[1 mark]**
> - In aqueous solution / in a solvent / from its constituent ions or molecules in solution **[1 mark]**
> 
> Answers referring to the equilibrium constant for the dissociation of a complex are not accepted
> 
> ii) The stability constant expression for [Ni(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> is:
> 
> - *K*<sub>stab</sub> = [[Ni(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>] / ([Ni<sup>2+</sup>][NH<sub>3</sub>]<sup>6</sup>)
> **OR**
> *K*<sub>stab</sub> = [[Ni(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>] / ([[Ni(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>][NH<sub>3</sub>]<sup>6</sup>) **[1 mark]**
> 
> Water is not included in the denominator unless the hexaaqua ion is treated as the reactant

> **[exam-tip]**
> When writing a stability constant expression, write the complex formation equation first to identify which species appear in the numerator and denominator and the correct power for each ligand.
> 
> A common mistake is forgetting the ligand coefficient. Here, six ammonia molecules coordinate to the nickel ion, so [NH<sub>3</sub>] must be raised to the power of 6.

parts.problem_md:
Ethane-1,2-diamine (represented as en) is a bidentate ligand.

Nickel(II) forms the complex ion [Ni(en)<sub>3</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>. This complex exists as two stereoisomers.

i) Define the term bidentate ligand.

[2]

ii) Draw three-dimensional diagrams to show the two stereoisomers of [Ni(en)<sub>3</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) A bidentate ligand is:
> 
> - A molecule or ion that can donate two lone pairs of electrons **[1 mark]**
> - To form two coordinate / dative (covalent) bonds with the same central metal ion **[1 mark]**

ii) The three-dimensional diagrams showing the two stereoisomers of [Ni(en)<sub>3</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> are:

![Diagram showing two nickel complexes with ethylenediamine (en) ligands in a distorted octahedral geometry, each carrying a 2+ charge.](assets/001-diagram-showing-two-nickel-complexes-with-ethyle.png)

**OR**

![Diagram of two nickel complexes, each with a nickel ion bonded to four NH2 groups forming a square planar configuration, with 2+ charge overall.](assets/002-diagram-of-two-nickel-complexes-each-with-a-nick.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a correct three-dimensional diagram of one isomer showing octahedral geometry, using wedges and dashes, with each bidentate ligand linking adjacent (cis) positions on the metal ion
> 
> 1 mark for the second isomer drawn as a non-superimposable mirror image of the first (same connectivity, opposite handedness)

parts.problem_md:
The complex [Ni(EDTA)]<sup>2–</sup> is significantly more stable than the complex [Ni(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>.

By considering the ligand exchange reaction between [Ni(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> and EDTA<sup>4–</sup>, explain this difference in stability in terms of entropy changes.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The difference in stability in terms of entropy changes:
> 
> - [Ni(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> + EDTA<sup>4–</sup> ⇌ [Ni(EDTA)]<sup>2–</sup> + 6NH<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - The number of particles / moles of species increases from 2 (on the left) to 7 (on the right), so entropy increases / Δ*S* is positive **[1 mark]**
> - The positive Δ*S* makes Δ*G* more negative (via Δ*G* = Δ*H* − *T*Δ*S*), making the ligand exchange more feasible / the EDTA complex more stable **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The chelate effect: polydentate ligands like EDTA displace multiple monodentate ligands in a single exchange step, increasing the total number of particles in solution and therefore increasing entropy.
> 
> Even if the enthalpy changes are similar, the more positive Δ*S* for EDTA displacement makes Δ*G* more negative, favouring formation of [Ni(EDTA)]<sup>2–</sup>.

parts.problem_md:
When chromium(III) sulfate dissolves in water, a violet solution containing the [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> ion forms.

i) State the bond angles found in this complex ion.

[1]

ii) Explain why the chromium(III) complex ion is coloured.

[4]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The bond angle is:
> 
> - 90° **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> is octahedral as six identical water ligands arranged symmetrically around the Cr<sup>3+</sup> ion. All six ligand-metal-ligand bond angles between adjacent ligands are 90°.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The chromium(III) complex ion is coloured because:
> 
> - The water ligands cause the 3d orbitals to split into two energy levels of different energies **[1 mark]**
> - Light / radiation in the visible region of the electromagnetic spectrum is absorbed **[1 mark]**
> - The absorbed energy promotes electrons from the lower 3d energy level to the higher 3d energy level **[1 mark]**
> - The complementary colour / violet light is transmitted / observed **[1 mark]**
> 
> 'Green light is transmitted' is not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> In an isolated transition metal atom the five 3d orbitals are degenerate (equal energy). When a complex ion forms, the ligands split the 3d orbitals into two energy levels. Light of a wavelength matching this energy gap is absorbed, promoting an electron to the higher level. The remaining complementary colour is transmitted and observed.
> 
> A common error is to state that colour arises because electrons 'return to their ground state and emit light', but this describes emission spectra (flame tests), not complex ion colour.
> 
> Also note: the question specifies [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>, which appears violet, not green. Stating the wrong transmitted colour will lose the final mark.

parts.problem_md:
Ethylenediaminetetraacetate, EDTA<sup>4−</sup>, shown in Fig. 1.1, is a polydentate ligand.

![Structural formula of EDTA showing two nitrogen atoms each connected to two CH2COO- groups and linked by an ethylene bridge](assets/003-structural-formula-of-edta-showing-two-nitrogen-.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

When a solution of EDTA<sup>4−</sup> is added to a solution of [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> ions, a new complex ion is formed.

[Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> + EDTA<sup>4–</sup> ⇌ [Cr(EDTA)]<sup>–</sup> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O

i) Name the type of reaction occurring here.

[1]

ii) Write an expression for the stability constant, *K*<sub>stab</sub>, of [Cr(EDTA)]<sup>–</sup> in this reaction.

[1]

iii) The numerical value of the *K*<sub>stab</sub> of [Cr(EDTA)]<sup>–</sup> is 2.51 × 10<sup>23</sup> in this reaction.

Suggest what this indicates about the position and entropy of the equilibrium.

[3]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The type of reaction occuring is:
> 
> - Ligand exchange / substitution / displacement / replacement **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The stability constant expression for [Cr(EDTA)]<sup>–</sup> is:
> 
> - *K*<sub>stab</sub> = [[Cr(EDTA)]<sup>–</sup>] / ([[Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>][EDTA<sup>4–</sup>]) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Identify the product ([Cr(EDTA)]<sup>–</sup>) and the two reactants ([Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> and EDTA<sup>4–</sup>) from the equation given in the question. Write the product concentration in the numerator and the reactant concentrations in the denominator. Water is excluded as the solvent.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> iii) The large value of *K*<sub>stab</sub> for [Cr(EDTA)]<sup>–</sup> indicates:
> 
> - The equilibrium lies far to the right / [Cr(EDTA)]<sup>–</sup> is more stable than [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>
> **OR**
> The forward reaction is very feasible / spontaneous / goes to completion **[1 mark]**
> - Δ*S*<sub>system</sub> is positive / entropy increases **[1 mark]**
> - The number of moles / particles increases from 2 (reactants) to 7 (products)
> **OR**
> 2 moles of reactants form 7 moles of products **[1 mark]**
> 
> Explaining only the entropy change without addressing the position of equilibrium is not accepted for full marks

> **[exam-tip]**
> A large *K*<sub>stab</sub> means the equilibrium strongly favours products.
> 
> The entropy change follows from the ligand exchange equation: 2 species on the left (the hexaaqua complex and EDTA<sup>4–</sup>) produce 7 on the right (1 Cr-EDTA complex + 6 water molecules), so the number of particles increases and Δ*S* is positive.
> 
> This is the chelate effect: replacing six monodentate ligands with one hexadentate ligand in a single step greatly increases entropy and drives the reaction forward.

parts.problem_md:
Chromium(III) picolinate, shown in Fig. 1.2, is a neutral complex that can be prepared from the weak acid, picolinic acid.

![Structural formula of chromium(III) picolinate showing a Cr3+ ion coordinated to three picolinate ligands in an octahedral arrangement](assets/004-structural-formula-of-chromium-iii-picolinate-sh.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

Chromium(III) picolinate is used in tablets as a nutritional supplement for chromium.

i) Draw the structure of the ligand in chromium(III) picolinate.

[1]

ii) A typical tablet of chromium(III) picolinate contains 200 μg of chromium.

Calculate the mass, in g, of chromium(III) picolinate in a typical tablet. Give your answer to three significant figures. Show your working.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
i) The structure of the ligand in chromium(III) picolinate is:

![Structure of the picolinate ligand showing a pyridine ring with a deprotonated carboxylate group (COO–) at the 2-position, and a lone pair on the nitrogen for coordination](assets/005-structure-of-the-picolinate-ligand-showing-a-pyr.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the picolinate ligand: pyridine ring with deprotonated carboxylate (COO<sup>–</sup>) at position 2, without a negative charge on the nitrogen
> 
> The negative charge on the nitrogen is not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> The picolinate ligand is picolinic acid (pyridine-2-carboxylic acid) after deprotonation of the COOH group.
> 
> Three of nitrogen's five valence electrons are used in bonding within the pyridine ring, leaving a lone pair that forms the coordinate bond with Cr<sup>3+</sup>.
> 
> The nitrogen does not carry a formal negative charge, only the carboxylate oxygen does.

ii) To calculate the mass, in g, of chromium(III) picolinate in a typical tablet:

- State the *M*<sub>r</sub> of chromium(III) picolinate:

*M*<sub>r</sub> = 418.0

- Calculate moles of chromium (1 μg = 10<sup>–6</sup> g):

n(Cr) = $\frac{200\times10^{-6}}{52.0}$

n(Cr) = 3.85 x 10<sup>–6</sup> mol

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate mass of chromium(III) picolinate:

mass = 3.85 x 10<sup>–6</sup> x 418.0

mass = **1.61 x 10**<sup>**–3**</sup> g **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for *M*<sub>r</sub>(chromium(III) picolinate) = 418.0 **AND** moles of chromium = 3.85 x 10<sup>–6</sup> mol
> 
> 1 mark for mass = 1.61 x 10<sup>–3</sup> g (to 3 s.f.)

> **[exam-tip]**
> The *M*<sub>r</sub> of chromium(III) picolinate requires care: the picolinate ligand has *M*<sub>r</sub> = 122.1, and three coordinate to the Cr<sup>3+</sup> ion (plus one proton lost per ligand), giving *M*<sub>r</sub> = 52.0 + (3 x 122.0) = 418.0. Remember 1 μg = 10<sup>–6</sup> g.

parts.problem_md:
Compound **L** is a complex with the empirical formula CrN<sub>4</sub>H<sub>12</sub>Cl<sub>3</sub>

The formula of compound **L** contains one chloride ion and a complex ion **M**, which has two stereoisomers.

i) Deduce the formula of complex ion **M**.

[1]

ii) Draw three-dimensional diagrams to show the two stereoisomers of complex ion **M**.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The formula of complex ion **M** is:
> 
> - [Cr(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup> / [CrN<sub>4</sub>H<sub>12</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Compound **L** has the empirical formula CrN<sub>4</sub>H<sub>12</sub>Cl<sub>3</sub> and contains one ionically-bonded chloride ion. Removing this gives complex ion **M** the composition CrN<sub>4</sub>H<sub>12</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> with a 1+ charge. The N<sub>4</sub>H<sub>12</sub> portion is four NH<sub>3</sub> ligands, giving the formula [Cr(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup>.

ii) The three-dimensional diagrams showing the two stereoisomers of complex ion **M** are:

![Three-dimensional diagrams of cis-[Cr(NH3)4Cl2]+ and trans-[Cr(NH3)4Cl2]+ showing correct wedge-dash notation with 1+ charges indicated on both isomers](assets/006-three-dimensional-diagrams-of-cis-cr-nh3-4cl2-an.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a correct 3D diagram of one isomer with 4NH<sub>3</sub> and 2Cl ligands, correct wedge-dash notation, and 1+ charge shown
> 
> 1 mark for the second isomer drawn as the other geometric isomer (*cis* or *trans*), correctly labelled, with 1+ charge shown

> **[exam-tip]**
> [Cr(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup> is octahedral and exists as *cis* (both Cl adjacent, 90° apart) and *trans* (both Cl opposite, 180° apart) isomers. Draw each with 2 'out wedges', 2 'in wedges', and 2 bonds in the plane of the paper.
> 
> Make sure the 1+ charge appears on both structures. A common error is to omit the charge or to draw cis and trans incorrectly by placing the Cl ligands in the wrong positions.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The stability constant, *K*<sub>stab</sub>, is:
> 
> - The equilibrium constant for the formation of a complex ion (from a central metal ion and ligands) **[1 mark]**
> - In aqueous solution / in a solvent / from its constituent ions or molecules in solution **[1 mark]**
> 
> Answers referring to the equilibrium constant for the dissociation of a complex are not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> A complete definition requires two elements: that *K*<sub>stab</sub> is an equilibrium constant, and that it refers specifically to the formation (not dissociation) of a complex ion in solution.
> 
> Writing only 'equilibrium constant for a complex' without specifying formation is not accepted for full marks.

parts.problem_md:
Silver forms different complexes. The stability constant, *K*<sub>stab</sub>, values at 298 K are shown in Table 3.1

**Table 3.1**

| **complex** | **stability constant, *****K***<sub>**stab**</sub> |
|---|---|
| [Ag(CN)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>–</sup> | 5.3 x 10<sup>18</sup> |
| [Ag(NH<sub>3</sub>)]<sup>+</sup> | 1.7 x 10<sup>7</sup> |
| [Ag(S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>3–</sup> | 2.9 x 10<sup>13</sup> |

The following equilibrium exists between two complex ions of silver in the +1 oxidation state.

Ag<sup>+</sup> + NH<sub>3</sub> ⇌ [Ag(NH<sub>3</sub>)]<sup>+</sup>

i) Write the expression for the stability constant, *K*<sub>stab</sub>, for this equilibrium

*K*<sub>stab</sub> =

[1]

ii) When a 0.500 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> solution of AgNO<sub>3</sub> (aq) is mixed with 0.500 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> NH<sub>3</sub> (aq) the equilibrium mixture of [Ag(NH<sub>3</sub>)]<sup>+</sup> (aq) was found to be 0.4998 mol dm<sup>–3</sup>

Calculate *K*<sub>stab</sub> and state the units. Show your working.

[3]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The stability constant expression for [Ag(NH<sub>3</sub>)]<sup>+</sup> is:
> 
> - *K*<sub>stab</sub> = [[Ag(NH<sub>3</sub>)]<sup>+</sup>] / ([Ag<sup>+</sup>][NH<sub>3</sub>]) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Write the complex ion product in the numerator and the free metal ion and ligand in the denominator. Water is excluded because it is the solvent and its concentration remains effectively constant.

ii) To calculate *K*<sub>stab</sub> and its units:

- List concentrations using an ICE table:

|   | Ag<sup>+</sup> | NH<sub>3</sub> | ⇌ | [Ag(NH<sub>3</sub>)]<sup>+</sup> |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| initial / mol dm<sup>–3</sup> | 0.500 | 0.500 |   | 0 |
| change / mol dm<sup>–3</sup> | −0.4998 | −0.4998 |   | +0.4998 |
| equilibrium / mol dm<sup>–3</sup> | 2 x 10<sup>–4</sup> | 2 x 10<sup>–4</sup> |   | 0.4998 |

**[1 mark]**

- Substitute equilibrium concentrations into the *K*<sub>stab</sub> expression:

*K*<sub>stab</sub> = $\frac{0.4998}{((2\times10^{-4})\times(2\times10^{-4}))}$

*K*<sub>stab</sub> = **1.25 x 10**<sup>**7**</sup> **[1 mark]**

- State the units:

Units = **dm**<sup>**3**</sup>** mol**<sup>**–1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for ICE table with correct equilibrium concentrations: [Ag<sup>+</sup>] = [NH<sub>3</sub>] = 2 x 10<sup>–4</sup> mol dm<sup>–3</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for *K*<sub>stab</sub> = 1.25 x 10<sup>7</sup> (allow 1.24–1.25 x 10<sup>7</sup>; note: the table value of 1.7 x 10<sup>7</sup> uses different source data and is not the expected calculated answer here)
> 
> 1 mark for units dm<sup>3</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> / mol<sup>–1</sup> dm<sup>3</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> In an ICE table, the amount of [Ag(NH<sub>3</sub>)]<sup>+</sup> formed equals the drop in [Ag<sup>+</sup>] and [NH<sub>3</sub>]:
> 
> 0.500 − 0.4998 = 2 x 10<sup>–4</sup> mol dm<sup>–3</sup> for both reactants.
> 
> Substitute these equilibrium values into the *K*<sub>stab</sub> expression.
> 
> To find the units, substitute mol dm<sup>–3</sup> for each concentration term and cancel:
> 
> mol dm<sup>–3</sup> / (mol dm<sup>–3</sup> x mol dm<sup>–3</sup>) = mol<sup>–1</sup> dm<sup>3</sup>.

parts.problem_md:
[Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> reacts with ammonia to form a new complex. Write an expression for the overall stability constant, *K*<sub>stab</sub>, for the formation of [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>

*K*<sub>stab</sub> =

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

[Cu(H~2~O)~6~]^2+^ reacts with ammonia to form a new complex. Write an expression for the overall stability constant, *K*~stab~, for the formation of [Cu(NH~3~)~4~(H~2~O)~2~]^2+^

Table 2.1 shows the stability constants for each stage in the replacement of four water molecules for the [Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> complex

**Table 2.1**

| ***K***<sub>n</sub> | **value / dm**<sup>3</sup>** mol**<sup>-1</sup> |
|---|---|
| *K*<sub>1</sub> | 1.78 x 10<sup>4</sup> |
| *K*<sub>2</sub> | 4.07 x 10<sup>3</sup> |
| *K*<sub>3</sub> | 9.55 x 10<sup>2</sup> |
| *K*<sub>4</sub> | 1.74 x 10<sup>2</sup> |

i) Using Table 2.1, calculate the stability constant, *K*<sub>stab</sub>, and state the units. Show your working.

[2]

ii) Deduce what this value indicates about the relative stabilities of the two complexes.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
i) To calculate the stability constant, *K*<sub>stab</sub>, and its units:

- Recall that the overall stability constant is the product of the stepwise constants:

*K*<sub>stab</sub> = *K*<sub>1</sub> x *K*<sub>2</sub> x *K*<sub>3</sub> x *K*<sub>4</sub>

*K*<sub>stab</sub> = 1.78 x 10<sup>4</sup> x 4.07 x 10<sup>3</sup> x 9.55 x 10<sup>2</sup> x 1.74 x 10<sup>2</sup>

*K*<sub>stab</sub> = **1.20 x 10**<sup>**13**</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Determine the units from (dm<sup>3</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>)<sup>4</sup>:

Units = **dm**<sup>**12**</sup>** mol**<sup>**-4**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for *K*<sub>stab</sub> = 1.20 x 10<sup>13</sup> (allow values in range 1.19–1.21 x 10<sup>13</sup>)
> 
> 1 mark for units dm<sup>12</sup> mol<sup>-4</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> The overall *K*<sub>stab</sub> equals the product of all stepwise stability constants: *K*<sub>stab</sub> = *K*<sub>1</sub> x *K*<sub>2</sub> x *K*<sub>3</sub> x *K*<sub>4</sub>.
> 
> The units follow from multiplying four sets of dm<sup>3</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> together to give dm<sup>12</sup> mol<sup>-4</sup>.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The *K*<sub>stab</sub> value indicates the relative stabilities of the two complexes:
> 
> - The very large *K*<sub>stab</sub> value indicates that the tetraamine complex / [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> is (much) more stable than the hexaaqua complex / [Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> **[1 mark]**

parts.problem_md:
i) Some transition elements and their compounds behave as catalysts. Explain why transition elements behave as catalysts.

[2]

ii) Catalysis can be classified as heterogeneous or homogeneous. Complete Table 1.1 by placing **one **tick (`✓`) in each row to indicate the type of catalysis in each reaction.

**Table 1.1**

|   | **type of catalysis** |   |
|---|---|---|
| **reaction** | **heterogeneous** | **homogeneous** |
| Fe in the Haber process |   |   |
| Fe<sup>2+</sup> in the I<sup>–</sup> / S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>8</sub><sup>2–</sup> reaction |   |   |
| NO<sub>2</sub> in the oxidation of SO<sub>2</sub> |   |   |

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Transition elements are able to act as catalysts because:
> 
> - Transition elements have more than one stable oxidation state **[1 mark]**
> - There are vacant d-orbitals that can accept lone pairs from reactant molecules
> **OR**
> They can form dative bonds with ligands **[1 mark]**

ii) The completed Table 1.1:

|   | **type of catalysis** |   |
|---|---|---|
| **reaction** | **heterogeneous** | **homogeneous** |
| Fe in the Haber process | `\checkmark` |   |
| Fe<sup>2+</sup> in the I<sup>–</sup> / S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>8</sub><sup>2–</sup> reaction |   | `\checkmark` |
| NO<sub>2</sub> in the oxidation of SO<sub>2</sub> |   | `\checkmark` |

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for all three rows correct

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part (i), the two key properties that allow transition elements to act as catalysts are their ability to adopt multiple oxidation states (allowing them to act as both electron donors and acceptors in reaction cycles) and their vacant d-orbitals (which allow reactant molecules to form coordinate bonds with the metal).
> 
> For part (ii), a heterogeneous catalyst is in a different phase from its reactants. Iron in the Haber process is a solid while the reactant gases N<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub> are in the gas phase.
> 
> A homogeneous catalyst is in the same phase as the reactants. Fe<sup>2+</sup> ions and the I<sup>–</sup>/S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>8</sub><sup>2–</sup> reactants are all aqueous. NO<sub>2</sub> and SO<sub>2</sub> are both gases.

parts.problem_md:
A solution containing a mixture of Sn<sup>2+</sup> (aq) and Sn<sup>4+</sup> (aq) is added to a solution containing a mixture of Fe<sup>2+</sup> (aq) and Fe<sup>3+</sup> (aq).

Table 2.2 lists electrode potentials for some electrode reactions of these ions.

**Table 2.2**

| **electrode reaction** | ***E***<sup>**ɵ**</sup>** / V** |
|---|---|
| Fe<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Fe | –0.44 |
| Fe<sup>3+</sup> + 3e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Fe | –0.04 |
| Fe<sup>3+</sup> + e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Fe<sup>2+</sup> | +0.77 |
| Sn<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Sn | –0.14 |
| Sn<sup>4+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Sn<sup>2+</sup> | +0.15 |

*E*<sup>ɵ</sup> data from the table can be used to predict the reaction that takes place when the two solutions are mixed.

i) Construct an equation for this reaction.

[1]

ii) Calculate *E*<sup>ɵ</sup><sub>cell</sub> for this reaction.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for this reaction:
> 
> - Sn<sup>2+</sup> + 2Fe<sup>3+</sup> → Sn<sup>4+</sup> + 2Fe<sup>2+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required.
> 
> ii) The standard cell potential:
> 
> - *E*<sup>ɵ</sup><sub>cell</sub> = 0.77 – 0.15 = **+0.62 V** **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For the equation, compare the *E*<sup>ɵ</sup> values: Sn<sup>2+</sup>/Sn<sup>4+</sup> (+0.15 V) is less positive than Fe<sup>3+</sup>/Fe<sup>2+</sup> (+0.77 V). The less positive electrode acts as the anode (oxidation), so Sn<sup>2+</sup> is oxidised to Sn<sup>4+</sup>. The Fe<sup>3+</sup> half-equation runs in the forward direction (reduction). Balance electrons: 2 moles of Fe<sup>3+</sup> are reduced per mole of Sn<sup>2+</sup> oxidised.
> 
> For *E*<sup>ɵ</sup><sub>cell</sub>, use:
> 
> *E*<sup>ɵ</sup><sub>cell</sub> = *E*<sup>ɵ</sup><sub>reduction</sub> – *E*<sup>ɵ</sup><sub>oxidation</sub>:
> 
> *E*<sup>ɵ</sup><sub>cell</sub> = (+0.77) – (+0.15) = +0.62 V

parts.problem_md:
Hexaaquairon(III) ions are pale violet. They form a colourless complex with fluoride ions, F<sup>–</sup>, as shown in equilibrium **1**, and a deep-red complex with thiocyanate ions, SCN<sup>–</sup>, as shown in equilibrium **2**.

equilibrium **1:**

[Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> + F<sup>–</sup> ⇌ [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>5</sub>F]<sup>2+</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O

violet ⇌ colourless

*K*<sub>stab</sub> = 2.0 × 10<sup>5</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> dm<sup>3</sup>

equilibrium **2:**

[Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> + SCN<sup>–</sup> ⇌ [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>5</sub>SCN]<sup>2+</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O

violet ⇌ deep-red

*K*<sub>stab</sub> = 1.0 × 10<sup>3</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> dm<sup>3</sup>

The following two experiments are carried out.

Experiment 1: A few drops of KSCN (aq) are added to 5 cm<sup>3</sup> of Fe<sup>3+</sup> (aq), followed by a few drops of KF (aq).

Experiment 2: A few drops of KF (aq) are added to 5 cm<sup>3</sup> of Fe<sup>3+</sup> (aq), followed by a few drops of KSCN (aq).

i) State and explain the sequence of colour changes you would observe in each of Experiment 1 and Experiment 2.

[4]

ii) State the type of reaction occurring during the experiments in **(d)(i)**.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The colour changes observed are:
> 
> Experiment 1:
> 
> - Violet to deep-red (adding KSCN forms the thiocyanate complex) **[1 mark]**
> - Deep-red to colourless (adding KF displaces the thiocyanate complex) **[1 mark]**
> 
> Experiment 2:
> 
> - Violet to colourless (adding KF forms the fluoride complex), remaining colourless on addition of KSCN **[1 mark]**
> 
> Explanation:
> 
> - *K*<sub>stab</sub> of [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>5</sub>F]<sup>2+</sup> > *K*<sub>stab</sub> of [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>5</sub>SCN]<sup>2+</sup>
> **OR**
> 2.0 × 10<sup>5</sup> > 1.0 × 10<sup>3</sup>, so the fluoride complex is more stable and displaces the thiocyanate complex **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The type of reaction:
> 
> - Ligand exchange / substitution / displacement **[1 mark]**
> 
> In Experiment 2, the fluoride complex is not displaced by SCN<sup>–</sup> because the F<sup>–</sup> complex has the larger *K*<sub>stab</sub> value.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Work through each experiment step by step.
> 
> Experiment 1: the pale violet [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> turns deep-red when KSCN is added, forming [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>5</sub>SCN]<sup>2+</sup>. When KF is then added, the solution becomes colourless because the fluoride complex ([Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>5</sub>F]<sup>2+</sup>, *K*<sub>stab</sub> = 2.0 × 10<sup>5</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> dm<sup>3</sup>) is more stable than the thiocyanate complex (*K*<sub>stab</sub> = 1.0 × 10<sup>3</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> dm<sup>3</sup>) and displaces it.
> 
> Experiment 2: the pale violet solution turns colourless when KF is added. When KSCN is then added, there is no colour change. The fluoride complex has the larger *K*<sub>stab</sub> value and cannot be displaced by SCN<sup>–</sup>.
> 
> For part (ii), any reaction in which one ligand replaces another is called ligand exchange or ligand substitution.

parts.problem_md:
Solutions of iron(III) salts are acidic due to the equilibrium shown.

[Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+ </sup>(aq) ⇌ [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>5</sub>(OH)]<sup>2+ </sup>(aq) + H<sup>+</sup> (aq)

K<sub>a</sub> = 8.9 × 10<sup>–4</sup> mol dm<sup>–3</sup>

Calculate the pH of a 0.25 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> FeCl<sub>3 </sub>solution. Show your working.

pH = ..........................................................
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the pH of a 0.25 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> FeCl<sub>3</sub> solution:

- Find [H<sup>+</sup>]:

[H<sup>+</sup>]<sup>2</sup> = *K*<sub>a</sub> × [Fe<sup>3+</sup>]

[H<sup>+</sup>]<sup>2</sup> = 8.9 × 10<sup>–4</sup> × 0.25

[H<sup>+</sup>]<sup>2</sup> = 2.225 × 10<sup>–4</sup>

[H<sup>+</sup>] = $\sqrt{2.225\times10^{-4}}$

[H<sup>+</sup>] = 0.0149 mol dm<sup>–3 </sup>**[1 mark]**

- Calculate pH:

pH = –log(0.0149)

pH = **1.83** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for [H<sup>+</sup>] = 0.0149 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> (accept 0.01492)
> 
> 1 mark for pH in the range 1.8–1.83

> **[exam-tip]**
> For this weak acid calculation, use:
> 
> [H<sup>+</sup>]<sup>2</sup> = *K*<sub>a</sub> × [HA]
> 
> This assumes [H<sup>+</sup>] equals [A<sup>–</sup>] (both produced in equal amounts) and that the equilibrium concentration of the weak acid equals the initial concentration, since the degree of dissociation is small.
> 
> Here, [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> acts as the weak acid, so [HA]<sub>initial</sub> = 0.25 mol dm<sup>–3</sup>. Take the square root to find [H<sup>+</sup>], then use pH = –log[H<sup>+</sup>].
